title: Options and Greeks Assessment
description: Pricing, parity, payoff structures and the Greeks — the option-pricing material from the derivatives modules. All market data is clearly hypothetical.

questions.prompt: Black-Scholes call price: spot $S=100$, strike $K=100$, risk-free $r=5\%$, volatility $\sigma=20\%$, maturity $T=1$ year. (Two decimals.)
questions.explanation: $d_1 = 0.350$, $d_2 = 0.150$; $C = 100 N(d_1) - 100 e^{-0.05} N(d_2) = 10.45$. The tolerance allows small differences in normal-CDF precision.

questions.prompt: Same option as above. What is the call's **delta**? (Three decimals; between 0 and 1.)
questions.explanation: Delta of a European call is $N(d_1) = N(0.350) = 0.637$: hold 0.637 shares per short call to be locally hedged.

questions.prompt: Same parameters. What is the **put's** delta? (Three decimals; negative.)
questions.explanation: Put delta is $-N(-d_1) = -0.363$. Note $0.637 + (-0.363) = 0.274$... no: put delta $= N(d_1) - 1$, and indeed $0.637 - 1 = -0.363$. Put delta = call delta − 1 is the identity to remember.

questions.prompt: Same parameters. What is the option's **vega per 1% point** of volatility? (Three decimals.)
questions.explanation: $\text{vega} = S\varphi(d_1)\sqrt{T}$; per 1 vol point divide by 100. Full vega is 37.5 per 100%, so a 1% vol rise adds ≈ 0.375 to the price.
$\Gamma = \varphi(d_1) / (S\sigma\sqrt{T}) = 0.0188$: delta changes by ~0.019 per 1-point move in spot — the rehedging cost driver.

questions.prompt: Same parameters. What is the call's **theta per calendar day**? (Three decimals; expect negative.)
questions.explanation: Annual theta is −6.55 (−$S\varphi(d_1)\sigma/(2\sqrt{T}) - rKe^{-rT}N(d_2)$); dividing by 365 gives ≈ −0.018 per day.

questions.prompt: Put-call parity: $S = 100$, $K = 95$, $r = 5\%$, $T = 0.5$. What must $C - P$ equal? (Four decimals.)
questions.explanation: $C - P = S - Ke^{-rT} = 100 - 95e^{-0.025} = 100 - 92.6544 = 7.3456$. No volatility appears — parity is model-free.

questions.prompt: A call with strike 100 trades at 8.20 while the stock is 105. How much of the premium is **time value**? (Two decimals.)
Covered call: you own the stock at 100 and sell a 105-strike call for 2.50. What is the **maximum profit** of the position? (Two decimals.)
questions.explanation: Max profit = strike − purchase price + premium = 105 − 100 + 2.50 = 7.50, reached at any expiry price ≥ 105.

questions.prompt: Long straddle: buy the 100-strike call for 3.50 and the 100-strike put for 3.20. What is the **lower** break-even price at expiry? (Two decimals.)
questions.explanation: Total premium 6.70; break-evens are 100 ± 6.70, so 93.30 and 106.70. Below 93.30 the put's intrinsic exceeds the combined premium.

questions.prompt: Bear put spread: buy the 105 put for 6.00, sell the 95 put for 2.00. What is the **maximum profit**? (Two decimals.)
questions.explanation: Max = width − net cost = (105 − 95) − (6.00 − 2.00) = 10 − 4 = 6.00, realised at expiry ≤ 95.

questions.prompt: Volatility rises from 20% to 40%, all else equal. What happens to an at-the-money straddle's price?
options: It falls: higher vol means more risk to sell
It rises roughly proportionally to the vol increase
It is unchanged: parity pins straddle value
questions.explanation: ATM option value is approximately $0.4 S \sigma \sqrt{T}$ — near-linear in vol for ATM strikes. Doubling vol roughly doubles the straddle. Not *exactly* (the approximation drifts away from ATM), which is why option (d) is the trap.

questions.prompt: You are short an at-the-money call and delta-hedged with 0.637 shares. Spot rises 1. If you do NOT rehedge, your position is now:
options: short gamma: the hedge under-compensates the new delta
long gamma: the hedge over-compensates the new delta
questions.explanation: Positive gamma means the call's delta grew above 0.637 as spot rose; your static 0.637-share hedge is now too small — you are short gamma. This unhedged residual is precisely what gamma P&L (and the lesson's hedging-cost discussion) quantifies.
